Visit from a Small Planet FRONT COVER - A giant Betelgeuse snake glowers at its victims in Beetlejuice. To produce a wildly offbeat supernatural comedy with wall-to-wall effects and limited funding, Beetlejuice director Tim Burton turned to firsttime visual effects supervisor Alan Munro who assembled a choice team of cost-conscious independents willing and able to conjure up hundreds of effects shots for a very small portion of the film's $14 million budget. In charge of creature creation and makeup illusions was principal effects contractor Robert Short: providing opticals and miniature support was Peter Kuran of Visual Concept Engineering; and tasked with enlivening three highly specialized animation sequences were Doug Beswick, Ted Rae and Tim Lawrence. Together they assembled the fanciful imagery that helped make Beetlejuice the first big hit of the summer season. Article by Jody Duncan Shannon. 44 When Amblin Entertainment brought Batteries Not Included to Indus trial Light and Magic, visual effects supervisor Bruce Nicholson found the prospect of creating a family of pint-size anthropomorphic flying saucers both intriguing and challenging. Principal among the challenges was the need to create ships that could be photographed in real time on live-action sets and also in bluescreen environments under motion control. Most importantly, the imagery produced through employment of these two techniques had to be stylistically indistinguishable even when cut together end to end. Developed to support the effort was a sophisticated new wire rig and a winning array of flying machines brought to life via overhead wires, motion control, rod puppetry, stopmotion animation and go-motion. Modelmaker Thomas Conti attends to was photographed using motion control at Visual Concept Engineering. 6 * CINEFEX 34 In early 1986, a script composed by Michael McDowell and Warren Skaaren came to director Tim Burton's attention - a script which, by Burton's own description, was strange and absurd and even stupid. What many would consider its severest drawbacks, however, were the very elements that persuaded Burton to take on the directorial duties for beetlejuice. Like Burton's past projects - Vincent and Frankenweenie and PeeWee's Big Adventure - Beetlejuice was just off-the-wall enough to capture the young director's imagination. "I felt very in sync with this material," Burton confirmed. "It had the kind of abstract and unusual imagery that I like to develop on my own. All of its strange images and characters and the way they float in and out of the story really clicked with me. I felt comfortable with them." The Geffen Company, which was producing the film for Warner Brothers, obviously agreed that the material and director were a good match and Burton was signed on. Late in the preproduction phase, Michael Keaton was cast as the title character of Betelgeuse, with Geena Davis and Alec Baldwin signed to play Barbara and Adam Maitland. The Maitlands are a young, happily married yet childless couple who expend their nurturing energies on the care and renovation of their rambling Victorian home. Early in the film, the two are killed in an automobile accident - a sad turn of events, but one they adjust to fairly easily since they still occupy their house and are able to go about their day-to-day activities pretty much as before. The real tragedy for them comes when their home is sold to Charles and Delia Deetz, who move in with their troubled teenage daughter, Lydia. The Deetzes are everything the Maitlands are not - upscale and obnoxious - and the ghostly young couple find the prospect of cohabitation intolerable. Deciding to exploit their new status, Barbara and Adam make several attempts to scare the intruders from their home. It soon becomes evident, however, that - as ghosts go - the Maitlands are hopelessly unfrightening. Eventually they summon the help of Betelgeuse - a sleazy self-proclaimed 'bioexorcist' who ultimately brings more trouble than help. As scripted, the film was wall-to-wall effects - almost three hundred shots in all - yet The Geffen Company, having just come off the unexpectedly expensive Little Shop of Horrors, had mandated a relatively small budget. This, coupled with Burton's own preferences, led to a decidedly low-tech effects approach orchestrated by Alan Munro. It was a first assignment as effects supervisor for Munro - a storyboard artist initially interviewed to fill that role. Impressed with Munro's abilities and his vision of the film, Burton brought him on as both storyboard artist and effects supervisor. "Tim and I really hit it off at that first meeting," Munro recalled. "We had some mutual loves in terms of effects - we both enjoy funky effects films that are out of the mainstream. We also seemed to be of a single mind in how we visualized the sequences in this film - always going for the straightforward, quick-and-dirty approach. It was the only way to go since we were trying to make a movie that was full of effects for a very slim price." On Munro's recommendation, Robert Short Productions was enlisted for enlisted for most of the effects work - which initially was slated to be done almost exclusively in-camera and on stage. Before the project was over, however, the burgeoning effects load would also include opticals and motion control photography by Peter Kuran of Visual Concept Engineering, stopmotion work by Doug Beswick and Ted Rae and replacement animation by Tim Lawrence. "We went to more than one effects facility hoping to find the best people for each particular effect," Burton noted. "We didn't even approach the bigger effects houses like ILM - partly because our budget was so small, but also because we wanted to take a simple, matter-of-fact approach to the effects. What I looked for were people who had an artistic bent in doing effects, rather than just a dazzling technical ability. I like effects that have a little humanity to them." Even with Munro's enthusiastic recommendation, Burton was careful to determine for himself that Bob Short was the right man for the job. One of his major concerns was that the designs that he and Munro and visual effects consultant Rick heinrichs were developing could be translated faithfully from paper into three dimensions. "One of our specialties," Short related, "is being able to create exactly what is asked of us design-wise. As a test, we were given a maquette that Rick had done of a moldering corpse which we named 'Kissy-face.' They asked us to duplicate this maquette in full scale with all the acted that du actions that it would have to perform in the film." Kissy-face was intended for a sequence in which the Maitlands first come face to face with Betelgeuse. Having been lured into a surreal cemetery, the young ghosts are startled when the corpse springs out of an open grave and plants a big kiss on Barbara. Adam pulls the corpse from her and throws it to the ground where it is finally revealed to be no more than a marionette. Since their realization of the Kissy-face puppet would determine whether they got the full assignment, Short and company dove into creating a functioning, exact duplicate of the maquette. Like all the designs that Short would be given in the months to the mone that a come, the moldering corpse had not been rendered realistically. "The corpse is so outrageously disproportioned that you don't really think of it as being a corpse in a literal sense. Since it was supposed to be revealed as a puppet anyway, there was license for it to be as outlandish as Tim wanted." In keeping with the overall low-tech style of the film, Short began by taking the maquette and compressing it down on a xerox machine to produce in-scale photocopies. From those, blueprints were generated and scaled up to size. Next the action would cut to a medium closeup of the head which meant that the cables in the head and eyes - assembled by Fred Spencer and Don Matheson - could be manually operated while just holding the body. Then we would go to the hands grabbing Barbara and the head coming in, which meant that we could pop the arms off the main ghost and use them in conjunction with a second head that was articulated to look like it was kissing. Finally we would cut back to the reassembled puppet being thrown to the ground by Adam. Thanks to Alan's storyboards, we could concentrate specifically on those aspects of the puppet that would actually be used - there was no need to overbuild. It was a very economical, functional way to go." After three weeks of intensive work, the puppet corpse was finished. Not only did it have all the requisite functions, but it was also an exact duplicate of the maquette. Ironically, however, even though it secured the overall effects contract for Bob Short, the Kissy-face ghost would eventually be dropped from the film. A late rewrite called for Betelgeuse to pop out from the grave instead of his moldering marionette. Though bumped from the film, the Kissy-face ghost did serve as a foreshadowing of the kinds of outlandish creatures Short would be called upon to create for Beetlejuice. "We started realizing that the challenges on this show were going to be monumental when the designs started coming in and they all had this zany kind of feeling to them. We were faced with the problem of creating life out of things that didn't look like anything known to be alive! It was difficult, too, because we thirting designs were getting designs and doing our construction all at the same time - an overlapping process that ran for the next two-anda-half months. That's a whole different situation than when you start off and you have all your designs and you know what you are going to be building from the very beginning. Also there was hardly any overlap of research for this project. It wasn't the same creature going through several evolutions or several creatures that were basically of the same family or genre. Tim Burton's vision for the opening of the film was a series of helicopter shots of the real town that lead indistinguishably into closeups of the model - where suddenly a gigantic spider crawls up over the rooftop of the Maitland home. If properly executed, only the subsequent introduction of human hands would reveal the switch from real town to miniature. "The model was in eighty-seventh scale," Munro explained, "and we shot miles of footage - about seventy takes - trying to get the spider to crawl up the miniature house and move towards the actor's hands. It turns out that spiders are very pesky actors and they do very little on command. We were blowing at it and squirting water - anything to get it to move." Although a usable take of the spider was finally obtained, the shot of the model itself - because it had been photographed with a locked off camera - was deemed unacceptable to cut in with the live-action helicopter shots. "I had quite a dilemma on my hands. How could we do a long meandering overhead shot of a model in this incredibly small scale - hopefully without the audience realizing that they were no longer looking at the real town - and then have the camera naturally come to rest on the house just as this spider is crawling over the roof? I finally came up with two ideas to solve the problem. First I had Rick Kess and Jim Belohovek and Tom Conti build a fortyeighth scale section of the town for the overhead part of the move so we could get as much detail as possible. Then we did a short, forced-perspective blend from the forty-eighth scale miniature to the eighty-seventh scale house. The house still had to be eighty-seventh scale because we had a real spider and real human hands to deal with. We took the completed miniature over to Peter Kuran at VCE so that we could shoot it on his motion control rig, which enabled us to have a camera move end at a point where we could then sit and shoot endless takes of spiders doing whatever they damn well pleased until we got a usable take. Stupidly, I volunteered to catch the spider. About three takes into this process, the cameraman - Barbu Marian - asked the spider wrangler if these spiders had been defanged and the venom taken out. The guy said, 'No, but it's cold in here so they probably won't bite.' With all the lights in there, I figured things were going to start heating up pretty fast, so I decided to let the wrangler catch the spider for the other fiftysome takes we did." Needing supplies for the model, Adam and Barbara make a quick run to the hardware store - a trip that ends in disaster when, swerving to avoid hitting a dog, their car careens off a bridge and into a river. Rattled but apparently unharmed, the Maitlands return home only to find perplexing evidence that they may not have survived the crash. The point is made indisputable when Barbara picks up a miniature horse from the mantle and passes it in front of a mirror, creating an image in the glass of the figurine moving through space of its own accord. Barbara herself casts no reflection. To achieve the effect without opticals, the actual mirror over the fireplace was removed and the wall it hung on was reversed to face in toward the set. Geena Davis then stood on the outside holding a pony that had a twofoot-long rod extending from its side through the opening and into the mirror-image pony on the other end. "I'd originally thought about rodding the mirrored pony from behind and having someone echo Barbara's movements," Munro stated. "I also thought we would want to put a sheet of clear glass in to substitute for the mirror. But the more I thought about it the more I began to realize that when you look into a mirror, you are not really conscious of its surface - what you see is the reflection. So suddenly there wasn't a whole lot of logic to that approach. Production manager Don Heitzer suggested that we put the rod between the two ponies and that way their movements would always be interlocked. The idea made sense, but when I presented it at a meeting, everyone was skeptical. How could anything that simple and stupid possibly work?" A quick test with a couple of plastic reindeer proved the feasibility of the approach, so the final execution was turned over to Bob Short. "We used store-bought ponies, gutting them out and then heating the plastic up so we could alter certain parts to be mirror images. The horses had straight legs to begin with and we bent them so that they looked like they were stepping and the heads were turning, one to the left and one to the right. The mane was also chopped off of one and reconstructed on the opposite side. Then we did a custom paint job to turn them from Shetland ponies into Arabians. Finally the rod was connected. By running it from one thigh to the other - rather than stomach to stomach - it allowed Geena to pick up the horse by the haunch, covering the tail and the rod and allowing more of a mirror image to show through. Not only was this method less expensive than an optical, it looks better if it is done right because there is no second generation." Confused and frightened by these events, Adam leaves the house in search of answers. As originally scripted, what he finds instead is a great void - a vast blackness in which giant menacing gears churn steadily toward him. Since the original intent had been for the sequence to be shot entirely on stage, physical effects supervisor Chuck Gaspar and his crew had created fullsized gears approximately fifteen feet high. Though executed according to plan, the approach presented problems of scale and maneuverability. "The gears traveled only in straight lines on two tracks parallel to each other," Short explained. "So they could really only be used in shots where they were coming directly at camera or moving right past. To get the gears to swing around and come back at Adam, it was decided that miniature gears shot on a motion control system would be needed. We built the miniature versions out of acrylic - about twelve inches in diameter - and Peter Kuran shot them on the motion control camera." "The gears were lit in several ways by Kevin Kutchaver," Kuran elaborated, "who also sized them differently, used various speeds and put them in different places within the frame. Because the mechanical artifacts were to be part of a black void, it was possible to shoot them simply against black rather than in front of a blue screen. "Any matting that had to be done against Adam or behind Adam was very sparse, so we just went in and hand-rotoed those frames. The significance of the great void sequence was to point out that Barbara and Adam are unable to leave their home. In fact, the script had called for them to encounter a different but equally hostile environment with each attempt to exit - a concept that Tim Burton came to realize would put undue strain on audience comprehension. "I dislike the tendency of fantasy films to have so many story points that you can't remember them all. I think we would have totally lost people if Adam and Barbara had been in a different place every time they walked out of the house. It would have been too much of a distraction." Simplifying the concept considerably, Burton decided to drop all of the different great void environs except one - a garishly colorful sand planet inhabited by a gigantic sandworm. Even after the gear sequence had been scrapped, Kuran was able to salvage some of the plate photography already shot with Alec Baldwin. "We could have reshot Alec against bluescreen, but he was no longer available at that point. However, since he was against black in the original plate material, we were able to go in and roto him for those shots. So the live-action was the same, but the backgrounds were different. It is actually the first time you see the sand planet and it takes place at night - so even though it looks different than the other sand planet shots, it works as sort of a preface to what is to come." For the remaining sand planet sequences the filmmakers had planned originally to shoot all of the actors in front of a blue screen and then put the backgrounds in later. However, Alan Munro once again felt a simpler method was in order. "I was able to talk them into building a sand planet set that could be used with the actors right there. My feeling was that the sand planet had to be built anyway - even for bluescreen plates - so why not build it large enough for the actors to stand in front. Because we were dealing with sand we were going to have to build the miniature at a fairly large scale anyway - fifteen or twenty feet across - which was plenty wide enough for closeups and even medium wide shots, so there was really no reason to use bluescreen for every single shot." To illustrate the plausibility of his idea, Munro built a rough sand planet set at onesixth scale and then shot test footage using a Barbie doll to represent Barbara. Tim Burton and the producers were convinced, and the majority of the sand planet shots were thus achieved without resorting to composites. "I hired Steve Burg to build a forced-perspective set," Munro continued. "We dealt with the scale by just picking an eye level and building tables that started at two-and-a-half or three feet off the ground and angling up to six feet at a pretty steep rake. The set was about fifteen feet wide in the front - where the actors would be - and about twenty-two feet wide at the back end. Because the planet was strictly sand dunes and big rocks, it was a simple matter. All we did was build rocks in seven scales ranging from eight feet tall down to about an inch-anda-half and arrange them in diminishing perspective. Since the whole set was only twelve feet deep, the first two scales took up the first seven-eighths of the platform and the last five scales were crammed into the last eighth." The set was further enhanced with a foreground dune which concealed the lip of the platform and afforded an area on which the actors could walk. Unabashedly nonrealistic, the planet was to be covered with brilliant yellow sand which was eventually found and procured from an aquarium supply company. "We ordered eight tons of this bright yellow aquarium sand - and now I get Christmas cards from the company because I was their biggest client in fifty years." The predominantly yellow set was also dressed with twisted rocks of bright red and was backed up with a cyclorama that featured a rich blue sky with two planets looming overhead - one electric green and the other bright orange. "It was like Walt Disney had thrown up on you -just this incredible wash of color which made it difficult to create any kind of depth or atmosphere - but Tim was insistent that we do nothing to interfere with the vividness of the colors." Burton did however eventually agree that some atmospherics were needed to enliven the cartoonlike environment. Pete Kuran responded by adding some wispy clouds. "As originally photographed, the sky was pretty bald and the sequences came off looking not just cartoony, but phony. To alleviate the problem, we decided to add some clouds - which meant that in all of the sand planet shots where people or stop-motion puppets were above the horizon, we had to go in and roto every frame so that we could drop these clouds in behind them. What we used were basically dry ice clouds - nothing new. We have a black table and black floor and we run dry ice and warm water and shoot it upside-down at an angle so that there is always some kind of gravity movement in the clouds. The results are very spindly-looking - not at all like cloud tank stuff." After several unpleasant excursions to the sand planet, Barbara and Adam accept the fact that they are permanently housebound and settle into a routine of peaceful nonexistence. This routine is rudely interrupted, however, when the new owners of their home - played by Jeffrey Jones and Catherine O'Hara - come to inspect the property, raiding every nook and cranny and spouting plans to turn the quaint and comfortable house into a trendy showplace. Heartsick at the prospect, Barbara and Adam decide to try out their newly acquired supernatural gifts. When Delia and her tacky interior decorator open the door to

a closet, Barbara is inside hanging from a noose. Getting no reaction - and unaware that mortals cannot see her - she then reaches up and pulls the skin off her face, exposing a screaming skull with eyes dangling out of their sockets and a big grinning mouth containing twice as many teeth as should be there. "The skull seems to be based on Barbara's idea of what a skull would look like and what would be scary," Short noted, "rather than what a medical student's rendering would be. The upper part of the skull was made out of fiberglass to hold the mechanisms. The lower jaw, because it had to drop down and then extend a little bit further than a normal jaw, was made out of foam latex and then painted to match the fiberglass. The eyes had to spring out, but not straight out. They had to come out at a certain arc and then droop down, which meant that we had to find just the right kind of flexible rod to work with the weight of the eyeballs." Three puppeteers were required to operate the finished puppet - one for the body, one to control the eyes and a third to puppeteer the mouth. For the scene in which Barbara pulls the flesh off her face, a lifemask of Geena Davis was put over the skull apparatus. "We had done a generic head cast to use for other appliances, and on the same day we did a lifemask with Geena doing a grimace. We could have simply resculpted the generic face to give us the expression we wanted, but I've found that the closer one is to the original expression in the alginate, the better." On set, Geena Davis stood in the closet with the hangman's noose around her neck. With a grimaced expression, she reached up with her hand to cover her face - at which point a cut was made to the artificial head. "Geena was actually down on her knees, beside the puppet. On cue, she reached up and grabbed the facial appliance off the skull, so her hand matched and the movement was right. We had worried how Geena would react to all the makeup and effects work since she was in The Fly and had witnessed what Jeff Goldblum went through on that film. But she was really excited about having it all done. As a going. away present, we gave her a replica of her grimacing head." The 'cheap way' entailed finding a good false perspective cut point in the den set. "We took a board and slotted it for Alec Baldwin's head and draped a severed neck piece down the front of it under his chin. So the fake desk face and the head were in the foreground, and the real desk was behind them." Body parts for the sequence were produced at Bob Short's facility. "First we just made a foam rubber corpse with a neck stump to lie on the floor. We did fairly detailed latex hands for that, but the rest of it was just a stock foam body from the shop. Then we built a slightly articulated head for the initial shot of Barbara holding the head. Alec Baldwin came in so that we could do a lifemask of him with a moaning expression on his face. I used a technique I had previously developed whereby we bypass the sculpting and molding phases and go directly to a fiberglass positive. We pour the fiberglass right into the alginate and then use Bond-o and other materials to reform the expression where needed. It gives a much better look than rubber and we have a completed lifemask in about three hours. Not only did this process give us a very quick and good likeness of Alec, but it instantly gave us a base in which to integrate the mechanics. We put cabling for the eyes up into the top of the head so that Geena could slip her fingers through a couple of rings that allowed her to make the eyes move left or right. Since someone was holding the head anyway, it made sense to let that person operate it instead of going to a remote control system." Short and his team next turned to rigging a realistic, headless body that could run upstairs. "Headless bodies in the past have either been animated or done with a guy in a suit that is one head too tall." Unable to employ the former technique and determined to avoid the latter, Short devised a variety of shots that, blended together correctly, would convincingly sell the idea of a moving headless body. "For shots from the back we had a neck stump rig that fit on the back of a stuntman at shoulder level. If the stuntman kept his head tucked down - leaning forward at a ninety-degree angle to his body - then from the back the neck stump was at the proper height and looked natural. For the running shots we created a fiberglass torso that one of our guys was able to wear above his own head. Inside was a direct cable system - built by Mike Moore - that the person who was wearing the torso was able to operate. As the operator's arms moved back and forth, the arms of the torso above would move back and forth in unison. 'We discovered that by enlarging all the teeth on the zipper so that they did not actually interlock and by cutting the back of the slide off, we could actually stick the slide on and have somebody grab it from its starting position, pull it across the zipper and then stop on the other side. We tried every combination of distributing the weight and balance on the truck to get it to land on four wheels and take off, but it crashed every time. It was about one o'clock in the morning and we had completely run out of ideas. Achieving this grand finale required a combination of miniatures, bluescreen elements and stop-motion animation. "The only problem with shooting the worm crashing through the ceiling," revealed Munro, "was that the snout of the worm stuck out quite a bit from where the Barbara puppet was sitting. Consequently the first time we ran cameras and had the sandworm bash through the ceiling, the whole thing stopped before you could even see Barbara. For the next take, we very carefully scored the ceiling and then took a broomstick and taped some debris on it. As the nose went through the second time, I slammed this debris piece through to bash the ceiling away enough so that we would get a glimpse of Barbara riding on top." "Next we needed a shot of the worm eating Betelgeuse and bashing its way through the floor," explained Munro. "Nobody wanted to be like Ray Harryhausen and animate all these little pieces of floorboard and debris, so a miniature floor section and a miniature pair of Betelgeuse legs were constructed. We shot it with the large scale sandworm puppet that Bob had built and

just had it set on an axis so we could slam it down head first. The jaw was puppeteered to make it bite and then bash through. In retaliation, the witch doctor sprinkles a fine powder over Betelgeuse's head causing it to shrink down to the size of a grapefruit. Later we did a roto which cut his head off at that exact point and then did a camera move on it to lift it off his shoulders." Preview response was used to determine which of the two endings would earn a permanent place in the film. Maybe cheap, maybe cheesy, maybe off-the-cuff - yet, the sheer volume of effects completed for Beetlejuice, as well as the ingenuity involved in bringing them off, make them worthy of respect. For Tim Burton, the project was a learning experience. "I was not prepared for the difficulty involved in doing the effects for this show, and the experience has changed my mind as to how I would approach them in the future. But I'm really happy with the way it has turned out.
